core: The working definition of the break-even point, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: the dollar amount or production level at which the company has recovered all variable and fixed costs — where total cost equals total revenue, no profit, no loss
THE formula: break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit), with each part named
Contribution margin: price minus variable cost per unit — the amount each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs — stated simply
The original worked example: a food cart's fixed costs, price, and variable cost per unit (Marisol's Curbside Kitchen, fictional)
Why break-even matters: pricing, planning, and risk — one line each
Break-even in revenue: the sales-dollar version via the contribution margin ratio, one line
The limits: CVP assumptions — constant prices and costs — the honest note
The honest framing: break-even is a planning tool, not a promise — the reality check
supporting: OpenStax's logic chain: at zero sales the loss equals the fixed costs, each unit sold shrinks the loss by the contribution margin until break-even, and each unit beyond break-even adds the same amount to profit
OpenStax's universality note: break-even applies to manufacturing, retail, and service businesses, making it critical to managers, business owners, and accountants
OpenStax's risk line: no business can operate very long below break-even
OpenStax's Hicks Manufacturing worked example (225 units; $22,500 in dollars) and CFI's water-bottle worked example (10,000 units), corroborating the units and dollars versions of the formula
CFI's no-profit, no-loss point phrasing and its note that the break-even number sets the sales target the company needs to generate profit

claims.claim: The working definition: the break-even point is the dollar amount or production level at which the company has recovered all variable and fixed costs — where total cost equals total revenue and no profit or loss occurs (the no-profit, no-loss point).
THE formula: break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit), where the denominator is the contribution margin per unit.
Contribution margin per unit equals sales price per unit minus variable cost per unit — the amount each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs.

At zero sales the business loses exactly its fixed costs; each unit sold shrinks the loss by the contribution margin until break-even is reached, and each unit sold beyond break-even adds that same amount to profit.
Break-even can be expressed in sales dollars: fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio (e.g., $18,000 ÷ 0.80 = $22,500) — the same break-even point measured as revenue instead of units.

Break-even analysis rests on stated assumptions: selling price per unit remains constant, variable cost per unit remains constant, fixed costs remain fixed in total over the relevant range, all units produced are sold, and the sales mix remains constant.

The honest framing: break-even matters for pricing, planning, and risk — it sets the minimum sales target and shows how far sales can fall before losses begin — but because it assumes constant prices and costs, it is a planning tool, not a promise of results.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which break-even matters more — the units version or the sales-dollar version?
positions: Break-even in units gives a concrete production and sales count (e.g., 225 burritos).
Break-even in dollars gives a revenue target (e.g., $2,250 in sales) that is easier to compare with actual sales totals.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The two are the same point measured two ways, and they agree when the numbers are consistent. The lesson teaches the units version as THE formula, as required, and mentions the sales-dollar version in one line.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does break-even analysis predict when a business will actually make money?
positions: The formula returns an exact number, so it can look like a precise prediction.
Real prices and costs change — discounts, supplier increases, rent changes — so the number moves with the assumptions.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: OpenStax states the assumptions explicitly and the lesson presents break-even as a planning tool, not a promise: the number is a minimum target and risk gauge calculated from today's prices and costs, recalculated when they change.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (the page served directly). Supports: the break-even point as the dollar amount or production level at which the company has recovered all variable and fixed costs, with no profit or loss because total cost equals total revenue; the CVP assumptions (selling price per unit constant, variable costs constant per unit, fixed costs fixed in total over the relevant range, all units produced are sold, constant sales mix); the logic that at zero sales the loss equals the fixed costs and each unit sold reduces the loss by the contribution margin until break-even, with profit beginning on the next unit; the units formula (fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit) applied to Hicks Manufacturing: $18,000 ÷ $80 = 225 units; the dollars version via the contribution margin ratio: $18,000 ÷ 0.80 = $22,500; break-even applying to manufacturing, retail, and service businesses; the statement that no business can operate very long below break-even; and a hair-salon Think It Through example ($35 haircut, $20 variable cost, $3,000 monthly fixed). Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: break-even analysis as the point at which total costs and total revenue are equal, used to determine the number of units or dollars of revenue needed to cover total costs (fixed and variable); the formula Break-Even Quantity = Fixed Costs / (Sales Price per Unit − Variable Cost Per Unit); contribution margin per unit as sales price per unit minus variable cost per unit (book example: $100 price, $5 variable cost, $95 contribution margin); the no-profit, no-loss point phrasing; the water-bottle worked example ($100,000 fixed costs, $12 price, $2 variable cost → 10,000 units); the break-even number as the sales target the company needs to set to generate profit; raising the break-even point via cost increases and lowering it via price increases or cost cuts. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.
